  • Why is my period lasting longer than usual?
Trying to Conceive

Why is my period lasting longer than usual?

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A period that lasts longer than expected can be unsettling. Several treatable causes are possible, but the amount of bleeding, associated symptoms and chance of pregnancy matter as much as the number of days.

Separate the length of a period from the length of a cycle

A period is the time you bleed. A menstrual cycle is counted from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. A longer cycle and a longer bleed are different changes, even though they can happen together.

Many periods last about two to seven days. Adult cycle intervals are often described as roughly 21 to 35 days, with variation by age and individual pattern. Twenty-eight days is an average, not a requirement. The early years after periods begin and the years approaching menopause may be less predictable.

Bleeding for more than a week, a substantial change from your usual pattern or bleeding that disrupts daily life deserves attention. Duration alone cannot tell you whether ovulation occurred. A cycle outside a typical interval may prompt assessment, but it does not prove that an egg was released too early or not at all.

Check whether the bleeding needs urgent attention

Seek urgent medical advice for very heavy ongoing bleeding, particularly if you are soaking a pad or tampon about every hour. Do not wait to reach a fixed number if you feel unwell. Emergency help is needed if heavy bleeding comes with fainting, marked dizziness, shortness of breath, chest pain or severe weakness.

ACOG specifically advises emergency care when products need changing hourly for more than two hours and there is lightheadedness, dizziness, breathlessness or chest pain. This is an example of a concerning pattern, not a rule that other symptoms must wait.

If pregnancy is possible, unusual bleeding with abdominal or pelvic pain needs prompt assessment. Severe or one-sided pain, shoulder-tip pain, faintness or collapse can signal an emergency such as ectopic pregnancy. Bleeding does not reliably exclude pregnancy.

Some non-hormonal medicines change bleeding

Aspirin reduces platelet activity and can make bleeding heavier. It is an antiplatelet medicine, whereas anticoagulants work through other parts of the clotting system; both can be relevant to prolonged menstrual bleeding. Tell the clinician why the medicine was prescribed and when you started it.

Other anti-inflammatory medicines, including ibuprofen and naproxen, can reduce menstrual blood loss and cramps in appropriate patients. Their effect is different from aspirin’s, but they are not suitable for everyone. Do not add them without advice if you take a blood thinner, have relevant stomach or kidney problems, or could be pregnant.

Some antidepressants and medicines used for epilepsy may affect bleeding, hormones or contraceptive effectiveness. Effects depend on the particular drug and combination. Do not assume every medicine in a class does this, that symptoms must settle in three months, or that you should wait that long for help. Never stop an essential medicine abruptly to test the theory.

Contraception can alter the pattern

Combined pills, progestogen-only pills, implants, vaginal rings, patches, injections and hormonal intrauterine systems can change when and how much you bleed. Some methods are also used to treat heavy periods. Spotting or breakthrough bleeding is not necessarily a normal ovulatory period.

A hormonal intrauterine system often makes bleeding lighter over time, although irregular bleeding can occur initially. A copper IUD can make periods heavier or longer. Contraceptive injections may produce irregular or prolonged bleeding in some people and little or no bleeding in others.

When a pattern changes, note the method, start date, missed doses, other medicines and any pain or discharge. A clinician can assess whether the change fits the method or whether pregnancy, infection or another cause needs checking. New persistent bleeding after a previously stable pattern should not automatically be attributed to contraception.

Delayed or absent ovulation is one possible cause

Hormonal changes can alter when an ovary releases an egg, or a cycle may occur without ovulation. The uterine lining can then shed unpredictably, sometimes after a longer gap and sometimes with prolonged or heavy bleeding. Ovulation does not always happen exactly halfway through a cycle.

Stress, thyroid disease, polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, breastfeeding and some medicines can be relevant. Changes in basal body temperature, cervical mucus or lower abdominal sensations may help someone notice a pattern, but they do not confirm the cause of delayed ovulation on their own.

Track the dates and symptoms if it helps, but do not use an app’s prediction as a diagnosis or assume a prolonged bleed means you cannot become pregnant. Persistent irregularity, very long gaps or difficulty conceiving can justify a discussion about hormonal and reproductive assessment.

Emergency contraception may affect the next bleed

Emergency contraceptive pills work mainly by delaying or preventing ovulation. The next period may arrive earlier or later than expected, and the amount or duration of bleeding can differ. Spotting and cramps can also occur. These changes do not show whether the method worked.

Take a pregnancy test from the first day of a missed period, or at least 21 days after the most recent unprotected sex if you are unsure when a period is due. Sex after taking an emergency pill can create a new pregnancy risk, so follow the advice given about ongoing contraception.

Do not assume every later episode of prolonged bleeding is an after-effect of one emergency pill. Seek advice if the change persists, bleeding is heavy or pain develops. A negative test taken too early may need repeating at the appropriate time.

Bleeding after pregnancy loss or abortion is not the next period

Bleeding immediately after miscarriage or abortion is related to the pregnancy ending and the uterus recovering. It is different from the next menstrual period. Its amount and duration vary with the pregnancy, treatment and individual recovery, so follow the instructions from the care team.

The first later period may differ from your usual one, and hormones can take time to settle. There is no reliable rule that a procedure produces a short first period while medicine produces a long one. Bloating, headache, breast tenderness, mood changes or tiredness are also not enough to decide whether recovery is complete.

After miscarriage, a period can take up to eight weeks to return; after abortion, timing also depends on recovery and any contraception started. Ask your service if a period has not returned when expected, and follow its pregnancy-test plan. Ovulation and a new pregnancy can occur before the next period. Worsening pain, fever, offensive discharge, persistent pregnancy symptoms or heavy bleeding needs earlier help rather than waiting eight weeks.

Fibroids and polyps can cause prolonged bleeding

Fibroids are non-cancerous growths of muscle and fibrous tissue in or around the uterus. Polyps are growths arising from the uterine lining. Either may contribute to heavy, prolonged or irregular bleeding, sometimes with clots. They are not limited to people aged 35 to 50.

Fibroids can also cause pelvic pressure, frequent or difficult urination, constipation and back discomfort. Some people describe pain spreading towards a leg, but this is not specific to fibroids and needs assessment. Polyps may cause bleeding between periods or after menopause and can sometimes affect fertility.

Ultrasound can help assess fibroids. A hysteroscopy uses a narrow camera to inspect the uterine cavity and can help identify or remove a polyp or certain fibroids. Treatment depends on symptoms, size, position and reproductive plans. Medicines or targeted procedures may be appropriate; removing the uterus is not the automatic next step.

Thyroid symptoms provide useful clues

An underactive thyroid can be associated with heavier or irregular periods. Other possible symptoms include feeling unusually cold, fatigue, constipation, weight gain, dry skin or hair, brittle nails and low mood. Appetite changes may occur too, but none of these symptoms alone confirms thyroid disease.

The pattern often develops gradually rather than as a sudden, unmistakable change. Mention symptoms beyond bleeding so the clinician can decide whether thyroid testing is appropriate. A thyroid test is not automatically required for every heavy period when there are no other suggestive features.

If thyroid disease is found, treatment should address it alongside the effect of blood loss, including possible anaemia. Do not start thyroid supplements or change a prescription based only on a period-tracking result.

PCOS, now also called PMOS, may cause long gaps and irregular bleeding

The condition traditionally called polycystic ovary syndrome, or PCOS, is now called polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, or PMOS, in current NHS guidance. It involves hormone and metabolic patterns that can affect ovulation, periods, skin and hair. Both names may still appear in medical records and patient information.

Periods may be infrequent, absent, light or irregular, and bleeding after a long gap can sometimes be heavy or prolonged. Acne, increased facial or body hair, scalp hair thinning, weight changes and darkened thick skin around the neck, armpits or other folds may be clues. People do not all have the same symptoms or body size.

The condition is more complex than simply having too much of a male hormone. Androgens are present in everyone, and assessment considers the overall pattern and other possible causes. Long gaps between bleeds may require a plan to protect the uterine lining, even when the lack of periods is convenient.

Endometriosis needs assessment even after a normal scan

Endometriosis involves tissue similar to the uterine lining growing outside the uterus. It can cause painful periods, pelvic or lower-back pain, pain during or after sex, bowel or bladder symptoms, fatigue and difficulty conceiving. Some people also have heavy bleeding.

Bowel symptoms can include constipation, diarrhoea or painful bowel movements; urinary symptoms can include pain or altered frequency. These symptoms have other possible causes too, so noting whether they change with the cycle can help the consultation without proving the diagnosis.

Ultrasound can identify some forms of endometriosis and other pelvic problems, but a normal ultrasound does not exclude it. Persistent symptoms may need specialist assessment, further imaging or consideration of laparoscopy. It is incorrect to assume most cases are ruled in or out by a routine scan alone.

Adenomyosis is a different uterine condition

Adenomyosis involves endometrial tissue within the muscular wall of the uterus. It differs from endometriosis outside the uterus, although the two can coexist. Some people have no noticeable symptoms; others have heavy bleeding, severe cramps or ongoing pelvic discomfort.

A feeling of pelvic fullness, bloating or pain with sex may occur. Examination and imaging, usually ultrasound and sometimes MRI, can help assess the problem and distinguish it from other causes. Symptoms alone are not enough to know which condition is present.

Treatment may include medicines to reduce bleeding or pain and hormonal options. The best choice depends on severity, other conditions and whether future pregnancy is a priority. Surgery is considered individually if simpler approaches are unsuitable or ineffective.

Perimenopause can change periods but does not explain every bleed

During the transition towards menopause, hormone fluctuations can make periods closer together or further apart, lighter or heavier. Hot flushes, night sweats, sleep difficulty, vaginal dryness, urinary symptoms and changes in sexual comfort may occur at the same time.

Menopause often occurs between ages 45 and 55, but the transition begins at different times and age alone does not establish its cause. A new heavy or prolonged pattern, bleeding between periods or bleeding after sex still needs assessment. It should not simply be dismissed as an expected stage.

Once someone has gone 12 months without a natural period and reached menopause, any new vaginal bleeding needs checking, even a small amount once. Hormonal contraception and some treatments can complicate interpretation, so tell the clinician what you use.

What a clinician may check

Bring a record of bleeding days, flow, clots, pain and any dizziness or tiredness. Include pregnancy possibility, contraception, medicines, previous pregnancies and whether heavy bleeding has been present since your first periods. A personal or family history of easy bruising or abnormal bleeding may suggest a clotting disorder.

Assessment may include a pregnancy test, an examination with your consent and a full blood count to look for anaemia. Other tests depend on the history. For example, coagulation testing may be appropriate for longstanding heavy bleeding with a suggestive history, while thyroid testing is more useful when other thyroid symptoms are present.

Ultrasound, hysteroscopy or a sample of the uterine lining may be recommended for particular findings or risk factors. The aim is to identify causes such as fibroids, polyps or endometrial changes, including uncommon serious causes, rather than give everyone the same test panel.

Treatment should fit the cause and your plans

Options may include tranexamic acid, an appropriate anti-inflammatory medicine, hormonal treatment or a hormonal intrauterine system. Iron treatment may be needed if blood loss has caused iron deficiency. Suitability depends on pregnancy possibility, clotting risk, other medicines and medical history.

A polyp, fibroid or other identified condition may need a specific procedure. Discuss whether you want to become pregnant, because some procedures affect fertility permanently. A treatment that improves bleeding is useful only if its other effects also fit your priorities.

Contact a clinician when bleeding lasts more than a week, repeatedly differs from your usual pattern or disrupts daily life. You do not need to wait several months to ask. Seek help sooner for pain, pregnancy possibility or signs of significant blood loss, and agree when the response to treatment will be reviewed.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Bleeding duration alone does not establish whether ovulation occurred.

Medicines, contraception, pregnancy-related bleeding and uterine or hormonal conditions need different assessments.

A normal ultrasound does not exclude endometriosis; persistent symptoms can need further care.

How BeMama can help

Keep a practical record of dates, flow and symptoms, and bring your medicine and contraception details. Discuss how bleeding affects daily life and any future pregnancy plans.

When to seek help

Heavy bleeding with fainting, marked dizziness, chest pain or breathlessness needs emergency help. Possible pregnancy with unusual bleeding and pain needs urgent assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A period and a menstrual cycle are different measurements.
  • Bleeding over a week or a major pattern change is worth discussing.
  • Do not stop prescribed medicine without advice.
  • Pregnancy and postmenopausal bleeding require specific assessment.
  • Treatment depends on the cause, severity and reproductive plans.

Frequently asked questions

Does a period lasting over seven days mean I did not ovulate?

No. Prolonged bleeding has several possible causes. Duration alone cannot confirm whether ovulation occurred, although the pattern may help a clinician decide what to investigate.

Should I wait three months before asking about a medicine?

No. Ask sooner if bleeding is heavy, persistent, painful or concerning. Effects vary by medicine, and an essential prescription should not be stopped abruptly without advice.

Can an IUD make a period longer?

A copper IUD can increase bleeding or duration. A hormonal intrauterine system often reduces bleeding over time, though irregular bleeding can happen initially. New symptoms still deserve assessment.

Does bleeding after an emergency pill mean I am not pregnant?

No. Bleeding is not a reliable pregnancy test. Test from a missed period, or at least 21 days after the most recent unprotected sex when timing is uncertain, and seek care for concerning pain or bleeding.

Is bleeding after miscarriage or abortion my next period?

Usually the immediate bleeding relates to the pregnancy ending and recovery, not the next menstrual cycle. Follow the care team’s instructions and testing plan; heavy bleeding, fever or worsening pain needs earlier help.

Does a normal ultrasound rule out endometriosis?

No. A normal ultrasound does not exclude endometriosis. Persistent pain or other suggestive symptoms may still need specialist assessment.

Are PCOS and PMOS different conditions?

PMOS is the newer name now used in NHS guidance for the condition traditionally called PCOS. Both terms may appear while terminology changes; care should address the individual hormonal and metabolic pattern.

Is heavier bleeding always normal near menopause?

No. Hormonal changes can affect periods, but new heavy or prolonged bleeding still needs assessment. Any bleeding after menopause should be checked, even if it happens only once.

Will fibroids or polyps always need a hysterectomy?

No. Depending on the cause and symptoms, medicines or targeted procedures may be options. Future pregnancy plans should be discussed before choosing treatment.

When should I seek emergency help?

Seek emergency help for heavy bleeding with fainting, marked dizziness, chest pain, breathlessness or severe weakness. Severe abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain or collapse when pregnancy is possible is also an emergency.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
